title: Adjective Declension Matrix (Adjektivdeklination)
summary: Adjectives placed before a noun take an ending based on three variables: 1) What kind of article precedes it (Definite, Indefinite, or No article), 2) The gender/number of the noun, and 3) The grammatical case.

tables.title: Typ 1: Weak Declension (After Definite Article: der, die, das)
tables.description: Rule of thumb: In the 'pocket' (Nominativ m/f/n and Akkusativ f/n), the ending is '-e'. Everywhere else, it is '-en'.

tables.title: Typ 2: Mixed Declension (After Indefinite Article: ein, kein, mein...)
tables.description: When the article lacks a distinct case marker (ein Mann, ein Kind), the adjective must provide it (-er, -es).

tables.title: Typ 3: Strong Declension (No Article Preceding)
tables.description: With no article, the adjective takes the ending of the definite article (with genitive m/n exception: -en).

rules.name: The Marker Principle
rules.explanation: German demands that gender and case be clearly signaled on a noun phrase. If the determiner doesn't show it (e.g. ein in Nominativ masculine), the adjective must show it with '-er'. If the determiner already signals it (der), the adjective rests with a weak '-e'.

examples.breakdown: 'ein' has no ending, so the adjective carries the masculine nominative marker '-er'
'der' already shows masculine nominative, so the adjective takes weak '-e'
